entry.title: Match the spelling card's fields to the real Capybara+ export (#23)
entry.content:
Match the spelling card's fields to the real Capybara+ export (#23)

renderSpellingReview was guessing at the front/back layout. Read directly
off the real `Capybara+` note type's own templates (the maintainer pasted
both), it turns out to be wrong in three ways:

- The front's clue is {{example_translation}} — the TRANSLATED example, in
  the language the reader already knows — not the target-language example
  with the word blanked out. blankWord() was solving a problem the real
  card doesn't have; drop it (and the now-dead function).
- The letter-count dot row doesn't exist in the template at all — the
  Capybara+ "typebox" is just Anki's own {{type:lemma}} field, with no
  length hint. Removed, including its CSS.
- The front's part-of-speech line is `{{part_of_speech}}` plus the
  language name in parens, e.g. "noun (Ukrainian)" — not
  "noun · uk". Added the same uk/en → Ukrainian/English map the real
  template's own inline script uses.

The back now mirrors {{FrontSide}} + the real fields: the answer word big
and green (matching the export's `.answer-word` color), the untouched
{{example}} (safe to show whole now that the answer is revealed), and
{{example_translation}} again below it — the real template shows the
translation twice (once as the front's clue, once again on the back),
which looked like a mistake until checked against the actual card.

Kept, deliberately not from the template: the "Correct"/"Not quite"
verdict against the typed answer. Anki's own type-in-answer does a live
character diff inside the review app itself, not via any template field —
there's nothing here to port faithfully, so this stays as this app's own
substitute, shown rather than enforced (same reasoning as before).

Verified against the demo server + a Playwright screenshot of the actual
rendered front and back, not just read for plausibility.

entry.title: Fix pronunciation audio, the missing Spelling and English decks (#21)
entry.content:
Fix pronunciation audio, the missing Spelling and English decks (#21)

All three found by comparing the app against the real collection and a real
export, rather than against what the code assumed.

**Pronunciation had no reference audio.** Every one of the 190 pronunciation
notes has audio_url NULL, so web/app.js rendered no <audio> element and a
shadowing card had nothing to shadow. transform.py set it to None deliberately,
commenting that media "was deliberately excluded from the export" -- true of the
export it was written against, false of a real "Include media" .apkg, which
carries 190 capy_pron_*.mp3 files referenced as [sound:...] from ReferenceAudio.

migration/upload_pronunciation_audio.py carries them into a public-read
pronunciation-audio bucket and links each to its note by (lemma, language, kind).
Public-read because a plain <audio src> sends no Authorization header and a
signed URL would expire while a card sat open; the bucket holds nothing else.
It needs the service-role key, so it is a local CLI like the migration itself
(D7) and the maintainer runs it. Idempotent: uploads upsert by path and the
note update is a PATCH, so a partial run is repaired by running it again.

Verified as far as it can be without that key: the read half runs against the
real export (191 recordings found), and every text was hashed and compared
against the live table -- 190 of 190 notes will match. Only the upload itself
is unrun.

**Spelling cards had no deck and no exercise.** Anki pins the Capybara+ note
type's second template to Capybara::Spelling (244 cards, template #1, confirmed
in the export), so a note's two cards sit in different decks. This app derived a
card's deck from its note, which folded every spelling card into Ukrainian and
English and made the Spelling deck disappear from a list that otherwise matched
AnkiDroid's exactly. deckOfCard(noteDeck, cardKind) now decides that in one
place, so the deck list, the queue and the daily counts cannot disagree -- no
column needed, since a note has at most one spelling card.

Worse, a spelling card rendered exactly like a recall card: the answer printed
on the front, which makes the exercise meaningless. It now asks you to type the
word, with the row of dots AnkiDroid shows, the word blanked out of its own
example, and the answer graded on reveal. Grading is shown, not enforced -- the
four rating buttons are still yours, because an accent typed without the right
keyboard layout should not force an Again.

**The English deck was invisible.** D2 assumed decks are disjoint by language and
filtered every listing to the viewer's learning_language. 199 English notes
exist, and the uk learner could not see them -- while the AnkiDroid collection
the two of them share showed him the deck, which is how this was found. The
filter is gone. The consequence is the one D2 itself named: card_state is per
card, so two people studying one card share its schedule; reviews.user_id still
records who answered, so a replay can split it later if that ever matters.

Also: microphone failures now say which failure it was. "Denied or unavailable"
covered several very different problems, and the likeliest one in a Telegram
Mini App is that the client exposes no navigator.mediaDevices at all -- worth
saying plainly rather than blaming a permission nobody was ever prompted for.
An empty recording is caught here too, instead of surfacing as Whisper's
"empty transcript".

Three tests added, including one asserting a deck row's counts equal the queue
that pressing it opens. 159 pass (was 156). Verified in Chromium: Spelling
appears as its own deck, the prompt shows the translation with 11 dots for
"письменниця", the answer is absent from the front, and a wrong answer reveals
both the word and what was typed.

entry.title: Make opening a deck fast, and import Anki's leeches + undo (#19)
entry.content:
Make opening a deck fast, and import Anki's leeches + undo (#19)

* Read the due queue in batches instead of per card

Opening a deck cost two Postgres round trips per due card. getDueQueueWithPreviews
selected the queue, then asked getNote and getCardState once for each item in it,
so the Ukrainian deck's 96 due cards meant ~192 sequential queries inside the edge
function before the first card could render.

Store grows getNotes/getCardStates. The per-card methods stay — a single card is
still a single lookup, and submitReview genuinely wants one row — but anything
assembling a queue now asks in batches. Both return maps so callers never
re-associate results positionally, and a missing id is simply absent, matching
what the singular methods express as null.

getCardStates filters on note_id and discards the kinds nobody asked for: PostgREST
has no clean way to express "these specific (note, kind) pairs", and D17 caps a note
at two card_state rows, so the over-fetch is bounded at 2x and costs one query
rather than one per pair.

The same request was also re-asking settled questions. getDeckSummaries fans out
over the deck list, and each branch independently re-resolved the user's learning
language, re-read their scheduler config, and re-scanned the same 48-hour review
window. Those three are now memoized for the life of the store object, which
sync/index.ts constructs per request and discards — long enough to stop repeating
one request's questions, too short to serve a stale config to the next. That
lifetime is load-bearing and documented as such. The memo holds the promise rather
than the value, so concurrent branches of a Promise.all share one in-flight query,
and a rejection is evicted rather than cached.

Measured against a counting stub client, with the daily limit capping the queue at
40 cards:

  GET /sync/decks                19 -> 8 queries
  GET /sync/due?deck=Ukrainian   86 -> 6 queries

The due path was 2 queries per card plus a fixed cost; it is now constant.

Three tests added, including one that counts the reads rather than just checking
the output, since a return to per-card fetching is invisible in every correctness
test. 144 pass (was 141).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_014UbPTTY8nipgewSYte9kjv

* Import Anki's leeches, and add undo

Two more behaviours from upstream, both chosen because they fit this schema
without bending it.

**Leeches.** rslib/src/scheduler/states/review.rs's `leech_threshold_met`, ported
exactly:

    lapses >= threshold && (lapses - threshold) % ceil(threshold / 2) == 0

The half-threshold repeat is the part worth keeping: it fires AT the threshold
and every half-threshold after, not once and never again, because a leech that
was unsuspended and still isn't sticking is still a leech. Anki's own unit test
(threshold 3 -> 3, 5, 7...) is pinned here as a test, and the default threshold 8
gives 8, 12, 16 -- asserted end to end by driving a real card through the
scheduler rather than hand-writing lapse counts.

Only an answer that actually adds a lapse can announce one. Testing the count
alone would re-announce on every later Good, since a card parked at 8 lapses
reads as "at threshold" forever; Anki avoids this structurally by only evaluating
inside answer_again.

The default action is 'tag', not 'suspend'. There is no tags table here, so
tagging means the reviewer says so and changes no scheduling -- on a shared
collection a card that silently vanishes mid-session is worse than one that
speaks up. 'suspend' is available and tested. Neither needs a schema change:
detection is a pure function of card_state.lapses, and the two config columns are
optional -- schedulerConfigFromRow reads them through a nullish fallback to the
same defaults the migration writes, and `select *` omits a column that isn't
there, so the app behaves identically before and after it runs. The migration is
included but NOT applied.

**Undo.** The operation docs/DESIGN.md 4.3 was written for and never used. Since
card_state is a fold over reviews, undo does not need a saved pre-image: delete
the review and fold what remains. What comes back is byte-identical rather than
approximate -- fuzz is seeded on (card, reps) and both wind back too -- which is
asserted by snapshotting the whole row before the answer and comparing it whole
afterwards.

Two things it deliberately does not do. It does not clear `suspended`, for the
same reason suspension is not part of the fold anywhere else: it is a judgement
about the card, not a consequence of how it was answered. And it is scoped to the
caller's own reviews, so on a shared collection it can never delete a partner's
answer to the same card -- pinned by a test.

Offline, an answer sits in the local outbox rather than on the server, so undo
drops it from that queue instead of asking the server to delete a review it has
never seen.

UI: a one-line notice under the toolbar reporting what was recorded, with Undo
beside it. It does not auto-dismiss on a timer -- the reason to read it is to
notice you tapped the wrong button, and a toast that vanishes in three seconds is
exactly what someone looking down at a keyboard misses. It clears when the next
answer replaces it or when the deck is left.

Verified in Chromium against the demo server: notice renders 74ms after the tap,
Undo returns to the answered card unrevealed, re-rating it afterwards is accepted,
and the notice clears on leaving the deck. 156 tests pass (was 144).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_014UbPTTY8nipgewSYte9kjv

* Correct DESIGN.md 2.2: the bot's card write follows /learn, not annotation

The revision recorded on 2026-09-16 described capybara-bot mirroring its
`vocabulary` table into `anki_notes`. Measured against the live project, that
table holds 11,329 rows to `flashcards`' 776 — and /export, the path this
replaces, has always been built from `flashcards`. Mirroring the wider set would
have minted roughly fifteen cards for every one deliberately chosen.

The write moved to /learn, /learn top and the grammar assistant (capybara-bot
#83). This records why, so the wider target is not reintroduced as an
optimisation later.

entry.title: Make rating instant, and run the reviewer as a Telegram Mini App (#18)
entry.content:
Make rating instant, and run the reviewer as a Telegram Mini App (#18)

* Stop the reviewer waiting on /sync/decks after every rating

Closes #16.

The rating buttons were never the slow part. submitRating awaited the review
POST, then awaited refreshStatsStrip() — a GET /sync/decks — and only then
called advance(), so the next card could not render until both round trips
finished. Measured live, three runs: /sync/decks took 3.94s, 2.90s, 3.99s.

Two halves.

The next card no longer waits for the deck counts. advance() runs as soon as
the review is recorded and the strip refreshes in the background, updating in
place a moment later. The write still blocks, because losing a review to make
the UI feel faster is not a trade worth making.

And /sync/decks itself was doing far more work than the question needs.
getDailyCounts paged the user's entire review history — 3,804 rows here — to
find the ones from today, and getDeckSummaries calls it once per deck, so a
single request pulled that history three times over. It now reads a 48-hour
window: a study day is at most 24 hours long and the current one began at most
24 hours ago, so nothing that counts toward today can fall outside it, with
room to spare across a DST seam. Cards already being studied before the window
opened are found with one targeted lookup over just the notes actually touched,
which is what lets the seen-set stay seeded correctly. The counting rule is
unchanged and still matches InMemoryStore: a review is "new" iff it is the
first anki_reviews has ever recorded for its (note_id, card_kind). When nothing
has been studied recently — the common case — the window comes back empty and
no further query runs at all.

Scoping to a deck also stopped listing the deck's entire contents to build an
id set. That select was unbounded, so it was one PostgREST max-rows cap away
from silently dropping notes, the same bug already fixed twice in this file.
It now asks only which of the touched notes are in the deck.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_014UbPTTY8nipgewSYte9kjv

* Run the reviewer as a Telegram Mini App

Closes #17.

The same pages, opened from inside capybara-bot, authenticate with Telegram's
signed initData instead of the device token. No install link to keep safe, no
separate app to open.

The credential is verified rather than compared, which is the whole difference
between the two routes: a device token is a shared secret, initData is signed by
Telegram with the bot's token. src/telegramAuth.ts implements the published
algorithm, checked against core.telegram.org rather than written from memory,
because two of its steps are easy to get subtly wrong and both are pinned by
tests: the bot token is the HMAC *message* while the literal string "WebAppData"
is the *key*, and only `hash` is excluded from the check string — `signature`
stays in, since excluding both belongs to the separate Ed25519 third-party flow.
Tests sign their own fixtures the way Telegram does, so they exercise the real
algorithm instead of asserting against a hash this same code produced.

Nothing is stored server-side and nothing new is trusted. The Telegram account
maps to a users.id through function secrets, the same way the device tokens
already do, so src/auth.ts still needs no database and identity still lives in
configuration. Verifying a signature uses TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN as an HMAC key and
never calls Telegram's API, so this does not become a second consumer of that
token in the sense capybara-bot's CLAUDE.md warns about.

On the client, the app does not depend on telegram.org's SDK having loaded — it
is an offline-first PWA and a third-party script is exactly what won't be there
on a bad connection. Telegram also passes initData in the launch URL fragment,
which needs nothing external to read, so auth.js prefers the SDK and falls back
to the fragment, persisting it in sessionStorage to survive navigation between
pages. That fallback is not theoretical: the browser check below ran with the
SDK blocked, and the app authenticated anyway.

Verified in Chromium against the demo server: the ordinary PWA path still loads
its decks and still sends Bearer; a Mini App launch sends `tma` carrying the
right account; the credential survives navigating to another page; a fresh tab
with neither is correctly unauthenticated; and with both present Telegram wins.

entry.title: Enable row level security on the anki_* tables
entry.content:
Enable row level security on the anki_* tables

These were created without RLS, so the project's anon key — public by design,
safe to ship in a browser bundle, printed in the dashboard — could read and
write every row. Verified against the live project before the fix: an anonymous
PostgREST request returned all 1037 notes, 3804 reviews, 1278 card states and
both scheduler_config rows, and writes were open too (that path is how the
original Anki import was bulk-loaded). That is the whole vocabulary corpus plus
a timestamped record of when two specific people study.

No policies, deliberately, and not a stub to fill in later. Every legitimate
reader and writer is an edge function built with SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY,
which carries BYPASSRLS — checked all three before applying, not assumed. The
browser never talks to PostgREST; web/ builds every request against
/functions/v1 and holds no Supabase key. And D13 auth is a device bearer token
resolved in src/auth.ts against function secrets, so it never becomes a JWT the
database sees: auth.uid() is null for anything that could reach these tables,
and a policy written against it would read as security while denying everyone.

Verified after applying: anon reads return [], anon writes fail 42501, and
/sync/decks, /sync/due and /sync/stats all still answer with unchanged data.

entry.title: Report the all-time lapse count on the stats screen
entry.content:
Report the all-time lapse count on the stats screen

successRate can't answer the question it looks like it answers. 98.5% reads as
excellent whether it comes from 56 failures or 5, and it is the count, not the
rate, that decides whether the FSRS weights can be personalised: fitting the
model needs examples of forgetting.

This is the number to watch before trying to optimise again. Running the real
FSRS-5 optimiser against this collection at 56 lapses out of 3789 reviews
produced weights that beat the defaults on held-out log loss (0.0836 -> 0.0331)
and scheduled a card 23 years out after five Good answers — a history with
almost no failures teaches FSRS that nothing is ever forgotten, and log loss
rewards it for believing that.

Counts every Again, deliberately unlike Anki's per-card lapses counter, which
ignores a card failed during its learning steps. Every Again is what the
optimiser trains on.

entry.title: Roll the study day over at a local hour, not midnight UTC
entry.content:
Roll the study day over at a local hour, not midnight UTC

Everything that counts "today" — the daily new/review limits, the stats
histogram, the streak — bucketed by midnight UTC. Anki doesn't: the day rolls
over at a configurable local hour, 4am by default, and the current day doesn't
count before it (rslib/src/scheduler/timing.rs). The visible symptom was a
streak reading 0 against a review history AnkiDroid still counted, because at
8pm Eastern it is already tomorrow in UTC and an evening's reviews were being
credited to a day that had not started.

The boundary is expressed as a day key (YYYY-MM-DD), not an instant. Deciding
which day a review falls in only ever needs the key, and keys sidestep the one
genuinely hard part — converting a local wall-clock time back to UTC across a
DST seam. Nothing here ever does that.

time_zone is an IANA name rather than a stored offset because Eastern is UTC-4
in July and UTC-5 in December; an offset would be right for half the year. Both
columns are per-user, on the config row that is already per-user, because the
two people this serves are not reliably in the same country.

Additive throughout: the columns are nullable, the application falls back to
(UTC, 4am) when they are unset or absent, so the new code is safe to run against
a database that has not had the migration applied yet.

entry.title: Import three of Anki's real scheduling behaviours
entry.content:
Import three of Anki's real scheduling behaviours

Read against ankitects/anki's own source rather than from memory, and limited
to the three that a reviewer actually feels on this collection.

Interval fuzz. Every card graduating on the same rating was getting the exact
same interval, so a session's worth of cards came back as one lump: measured,
40 new cards learned in one sitting all landed on a single day. ts-fsrs already
implements Anki's fuzz ranges exactly (checked value-by-value against
rslib/src/scheduler/states/fuzz.rs) — it was just switched off, on the grounds
that randomness would break the "card_state is a fold over reviews" property in
DESIGN.md 4.3. That turns out not to apply: Anki's fuzz is a seeded draw, not a
random one. Seeding it the way Anki does, on (card, reps), keeps replay
bit-identical and additionally makes the interval printed on a rating button the
interval the answer actually schedules — ts-fsrs' default seed mixes in the
review timestamp, so the seconds spent deciding would otherwise change it.

New cards mixed into reviews, Anki's default new_mix. They were appended after
every review, which with a real backlog means a new word is only reached on a
day the whole review queue gets cleared. Intersperser is ported from
rslib/src/scheduler/queue/builder/intersperser.rs rather than approximated,
since the even spacing at the edges is the point.

Learn-ahead, Anki's learn_ahead_secs (1200). A card due in two minutes no longer
reports nothing left to study; it is offered after the rest of the queue, never
ahead of it. Two existing tests asserted the old behaviour here and now assert
the distinction between a card minutes away and one days away.

entry.title: Page through anki_reviews/anki_notes past PostgREST's 1000-row cap
entry.content:
Page through anki_reviews/anki_notes past PostgREST's 1000-row cap

getReviewsSince, getDailyCounts, getDueCandidates and getCardStateCounts
all did one unbounded select each. PostgREST caps an unbounded select at
its own server-side max-rows (1000 on this project) regardless of ORDER
BY -- so a select ordered ascending silently returns the OLDEST rows,
not the most recent, once a user's history crosses that cap.

Found live migrating a real ~3,800-review collection (2026-09-16):
/sync/stats reported totalReviews: 1000 against an account with 3789
real reviews, and getDailyCounts' "how many has this user already
studied today" count was silently blind to everything after row 1000 --
exactly the rows most likely to be today's.

Fixed by paging all four methods through PAGE_SIZE-sized .range() calls
until a page comes back short. getDueCandidates/getCardStateCounts were
still under the cap for this account (838 notes) but close enough,
against an account whose note count only grows (bot dual-write, scan),
that leaving them unbounded was just deferring the same bug.

Verified live: /sync/stats now reports totalReviews: 3789 (matching
`select count(*) from anki_reviews where user_id = ...` exactly) and a
correct successRate; /sync/decks' Grammar (6/0/7) and Pronunciation
(40/4/34) counts match the real AnkiDroid app's own numbers for the
same account. deno check and all 93 tests pass.

entry.title: Capture card_state.last_review in the migration output
entry.content:
Capture card_state.last_review in the migration output

card_state.due/state alone are enough to place a migrated card correctly
in the due queue, but src/review/mutations.ts's toFsrsCardState treats a
card with no last_review as brand new -- discarding every bit of migrated
stability/difficulty on that card's very next real review, silently. The
live schema's own comment on this column already says as much ("Required
to correctly resume FSRS scheduling, not optional bookkeeping"); the
migration output just didn't carry it.

Derived from the same card's own revlog already in scope during
card_state construction (the latest reviewed_at), not guessed at -- and
warns instead of silently leaving it null if a non-new card somehow has
no revlog at all (which shouldn't be possible: a card can only be
non-new in Anki because it was reviewed).

Verified against the real export: 1332/1332 non-new card_states now
carry a real last_review, zero "no revlog rows found" warnings. 59
tests (7 new), all against synthetic fixtures.

entry.title: Implement D17/D18 in the migration CLI: deck, spelling cards, pronunc…
entry.content:
Implement D17/D18 in the migration CLI: deck, spelling cards, pronunciation

migration/'s Python CLI has read a real AnkiDroid export cleanly since the
migration spike, but only ever recognized plain vocab notes as a single
undifferentiated pile — no deck, always kind='vocab'/has_spelling=false,
and it silently discarded the real second card of every Capybara+ note
(warned "expected 1 card", then just picked one and moved on) and skipped
every Capybara Pronunciation (shadowing) note outright. Both gaps were
already named and tracked (docs/DESIGN.md, README's own status table).

Deck and card_kind now come from where a note's card(s) actually live,
found empirically against a real export: a plain Capybara note has one
card, filed directly in its home deck (Ukrainian/English/Grammar); a
Capybara+ note has two, one in that home deck and a second filed in
Spelling — whichever card ISN'T in Spelling is the note's home deck, and
that's also how a card is told apart as 'recall' vs 'spelling' (deck
placement, not template order). Pronunciation notes get their own
transform (TargetText->lemma, Translation->lemma_translation, Hint->gloss,
deck fixed to "Pronunciation"), including the real, malformed case this
export actually has: 13 notes with an empty Language field and a garbled
TargetText (a CSV dump pasted into the wrong field) — skipped, not
guessed at, same principle as everywhere else in this package.

Verified against the real export (2026-09-16): 1285 notes recognized (13
skipped, all the malformed pronunciation ones), 1529 card_states (1285
recall + 244 spelling, matching the 244 real Capybara+ notes exactly),
decks Ukrainian 767 / English 266 / Grammar 61 / Pronunciation 191, zero
notes with a card_kind set that disagrees with has_spelling. 52 tests
(15 new), all against synthetic fixtures.

Still not done, deliberately, per this package's own invariant
(__init__.py): it does not write to Postgres and it never will — that's
a separate, later step.
